intro: Every day the dice pick a few words and the game has to make sense of them. Today's pile: a broccoli raised by wolves, sculpting snowflakes, a crank, a bet, an inspector. Here's how that turned into a snow lathe in the North Woods.

rolls.became: B. Roccoli fell off a farm truck as a seedling and was raised by the pack. It has floret ears, it howls when the Flurry goes out, and it learned to read from the filing cabinet of the old snow works in the den, so it only speaks in memos. Broccoli is a cold crop: frost makes it sweet and heat makes it bolt into yellow flowers, which is why it cares so much about snow.
The den has a 1927 snowflake lathe from the Boreal Snow Works. It has six spokes, so every cut comes out mirrored six ways, the way real flakes do.
You drag round and round to turn the lathe's crank. Every turn makes one cut. The lathe is heavy, so going faster than a turn and a half a second doesn't help.
This November Summer won't clock out. It bet the broccoli there'd be no snow this year. If the broccoli loses, it has to bolt.

The Bureau of Precipitation Standards says no two snowflakes may be alike, and the Inspector (an ermine in a bowler hat) keeps the ledger. That's real counting: with 3 notches there are only 9 patterns of 2 cuts, so once they're all on file every flake needs 3 cuts, then 4. A new notch widens every size at once and the minimum drops back.

Ida, the old she-wolf who raised the broccoli. She takes the den's little hand lathe. Her paw wobbles, so her flakes never match anything, and the Inspector passes every one without touching the ledger.

Summer sends heat waves, literally: A Warm Breeze, Re: Your Melt, Q3 Heat Variance, Kettle Week, the Heat Dome. Each one waits at the treeline. When you send the Flurry out, the fight runs itself, each flake cooling it by its chill and melting. You can keep cranking to send in reinforcements.

rolls.value: you pay with something you need
rolls.became: Every lathe part is pressed from ice, so requisitions are paid in flakes taken straight out of the Flurry, the same flakes you need for the next wave. Buy now and grow, or save up and fight.
Eight heat waves and a race, about half an hour. The pacing sim finishes in 22 minutes, and real people take longer.
The Flurry stands a few hundred flakes strong at most. Heat waves run from 8 heat up to the Heat Dome's 999 (the form only has three boxes), and the last race is a few hundred flakes onto the den.
A 1920s travel poster for a snow works: a sunburst behind the moon, stepped pines, a brass faceplate, Poiret One lettering and gold double rules.
Night blues and plums for the sky, brass and gold for the machine, frost and cream for the snow, rust for Summer.

Interlocking metallophones over a gong cycle in D major blues (D E F F♯ A B). That bluesy F/F♯ rub is the broccoli's attitude. The layers fill in as the waves get bigger and the tempo picks up for the race. Every crank click, cut and stamp is on the same scale.
The log is the broccoli's memos. Summer replies-all with heat waves, the Inspector circulates notices, and the pups unionise (their only demand is more turning).
Just a November with no snow in it.

After the Heat Dome, Summer calls time. Its thermometer climbs from 70°F toward 100°F, and every flake you or Ida make lands straight on the den. If Summer gets there first it demands a recount, and some snow melts.

The Inspector's final report counts who cut every flake. Ida, temporary, no employee number, cut most of the first snow, and not one of hers needed the ledger. She goes in the Employee of the Month frame. The 'Made: you · Ida' counter has been showing her pulling ahead all game.

outro: No snowflakes were duplicated in the making of this game. The Inspector checked.
